III. -- ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS:
The law governing resolution of this appeal can be summarized as
follows: All property is to be valued at one hundred percent of its
true and fair value in money. True and fair value is " market value,"
the price to be paid by a willing buyer to a willing seller. Carkonen
v. Williams, 76 Wn. 2d 617, 458 P. 2d 280 ( 1969). All real property is to
be listed and assessed with reference to its value on January 1st of the
assessment year. RCW 84. 40.020.
RCW 84. 40. 030 states that the true and fair value of real property
for taxation purposes shall be based upon the following criteria:

1 1) Any sales of the property being appraised or
similar properties with respect to sales made within the past
2 five years. The appraisal shall be consistent with the
comprehensive land use plan, development regulations under
3 chapter 36. 70A RCW, zoning, and any other governmental
policies or practices in effect at the time of appraisal
4 that affect the use of property, as well as physical and
environmental influences. . . . The appraisal shall also
5 take into account . . . the extent to which the sale of a
similar property actually represents the general effective
6 market demand for property of such type, in the geographical
area in which such property is located: . . .
7 2) In addition to sales as defined in subsection ( 1),
consideration may be given to cost, cost less depreciation,
8 reconstruction cost less depreciation, or capitalization of
income that would be derived from prudent use of the prop-
9 erty. In the case of property of a complex nature, or being
used under terms of a franchise from a public agency, or
10 operating as a public utility, or property not having a
record of sale within five years and not having a significant
11 number of sales of similar property in the general area, the
provisions of this subsection ( 2) shall be the dominant
12 factors in valuation.
13
14 The value placed on the property by the assessor is presumed to
15 be correct, and can only be overcome by presentation of clear, cogent,
16 and convincing evidence that the value is erroneous. RCW 84. 40. 0301;
17 Weyerhaeuser Co. v. Easter, 126 Wn. 2d 370, 894 P. 2d 1290 ( 1995).
18 Clear, cogent and convincing" evidence means a quantum of proof which
19 is less than beyond a reasonable doubt, but more than a mere prepon-
20 derance of the evidence. It is the quantum of evidence necessary to
21 convince the trier of fact that the ultimate fact in issue is " highly
22 probable." In re Sego, 82 Wn. 2d 736, 513 P. 2d 831 ( 1973). The presump-
23 tion of correctness applies only to the assessor' s original valuation.
24 It does not apply to the value placed on the property by the county
25 board of equalization. See AGO 1986 No. 3. Since the Assessor is

After considering the arguments made on behalf of both parties,
this Board now makes its decision as follows:
OPINION
In Valley Fruit v. Department of Revenue, 92 Wn. App. 413, 963
P. 2d 886 ( 1998), rev. den., 137 Wn'. 2d ' 1017 ( 1999), the Court of
Appeals, overruling this Board, determined that apple packers are
manufacturers," and thus can qualify for the then -existing distressed
areas sales deferral with respect to the purchase of manufacturing
equipment. RCW Chapter 82. 60; 82. 62. The Taxpayers had built
controlled atmosphere storage facilities and purchased apple packing
equipment in 1994, 1995, and 1996; but they had not applied for the
sales tax deferral prior to their investments because they believed
the Department would have denied their applications on the merits.
The Taxpayers now seek to compel the Department to accept their
applications and process them in accordance with the Valley Fruit
decision. We conclude the Department acted correctly when it declined
to process the Taxpayers' applications, and dismiss the Taxpayers'
appeals.
FINAL DECISION - Page 3 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

FACTS1
The Taxpayers are engaged inthe apple packing and controlled
atmosphere storage warehouse business in Yakima County, Washington.
Between 1994 and 1997, they made substantial investments in construct-
ing new controlled atmosphere warehouses and installing new apple
packing equipment.
The Taxpayers were aware at the time they made these investments
that Washington permitted manufacturers in Yakima County to defer
sales tax on investments in new manufacturing buildings, machinery,
and equipment, and permitted such manufacturers to credit an amount
against their business and occupation ( B&O) taxes with respect to each
new employment position created at their manufacturing facility. The
Taxpayers were aware that they had to submit applications to, and
receive approval from, the Department prior to making their invest-
ments or hiring new employees. The Taxpayers were also aware that the
Department did not consider apple packing and controlled atmosphere
storage to be " manufacturing" as that term is defined in the deferral
and tax credit statutes, and would therefore deny their applications
out of hand. Consequently, the Taxpayers did not apply for the sales
tax deferral or the B&O tax credit at the time they made their
Because this matter is before us on cross motions for summary
judgment, formal findings of fact are inappropriate. The " Opinion"
section constitutes the Board' s findings of fact for purposes of RCW
82. 03. 100.
FINAL DECISION - Page 4 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

investments and hired new employees. The Taxpayers paid the sales tax
and B&O tax without written complaint.
At the time the Taxpayers made their investments, the Department
and this Board had long been of the view that apple packing did not
constitute " manufacturing" for purposes of the B&O tax, and hence
did not constitute " manufacturing" for purposes of the distressed
areas tax relief programs. See Custom Apple Packers Quincy, Inc., v.
Department of Revenue, BTA Docket No. 39498, 11 WTD 289 ( 1991). In
August 1997, the Franklin and Yakima County Superior Courts decided
that apple packing was " manufacturing" for purposes of the sales tax
deferral. . Valley Fruit v. Department of Revenue, Franklin County
Cause No. 97- 2- 50028- 4 and Douglas Fruit Co., Inc. v. Department
of Revenue, Yakima County Cause No. 97- 2- 00080- 6. The Department
appealed, but it nevertheless immediately began approving- applica-

example, it approved an application for sales tax deferral filed
by CPC with respect to construction of a new controlled atmosphere
warehouse between April and September 1998. ( Ex. C, Alegria Affi-
davit)
In the wake of the Superior Court decisions cited above, the
Taxpayers filed applications for sales tax deferrals with respect to
investments made in new controlled atmosphere storage warehouses and
new apple packing equipment in 1994, 1995, and 1996. CPC filed their

16 purposes ( RCW 82. 04. 120) so as to specifically exclude " . the
17 growing, harvesting, or producing of agricultural products; or packing
18 of agricultural products, including sorting, washing, rinsing,
19 grading, waxing, treating with fungicide, packaging, chilling, or

Fruit: investments in apple packing equipment and controlled atmos-
phere storage warehouses do not qualify for the distressed area sales
tax deferral and B&O tax credits.
HB 2295 had one other feature which bears on the issues in this
appeal. It was made expressly retroactive. " This act is intended to
clarify that this is the intent of the legislature both retroactively
and prospectively." HB 2295 § 4. The bill took effect on June 7,
1999. HB 2295 § 5. The purpose of the retroactive provision was not
so much to emphasize the Legislature' s and the Department' s disagree-
ment with the Court of Appeals' interpretation as it was to guarantee
that the unpalatable consequences flowing from a logical retroactive
extension of the Valley Fruit decision would not occur. 2
2 After Valley Fruit, the Department was in a tight spot. On the one
hand, it arguably would have been required as a matter of principled
tax administration ( i. e., according to the language of the tax code)
to apply the Valley Fruit result to B&O and sales tax obligations of
all agricultural processors and farmers—including those not located in
distressed areas. See Determination No. 99- 351 at 4, Ex. A, CPC' s
Notice of Appeal. Further, it would have been required to apply the
result ( arguably) retroactively to all periods still open under the
four-year statute of limitations and ( certainly) prospectively from
the date of the Court of Appeals' decision. On the other hand, given
the importance of Washington' s agricultural industry and the State' s
historical policy of favorable treatment tax -wise as compared to most
other industries, enforcing the tax code remorselessly according to
the letter of the law would upset reasonable expectations -and cause
severe, and in many cases irreparable, harm to many people. Whatever
one may suppose about the Legislature' s intent in enacting HB 2295, it
is clear that one of the Department' s main purposes in sponsoring the
bill was to extricate itself from what it believed was a no- win
situation.
FINAL DECISION - Page 8 Dockets Nos. 00- 005 to 00- 009

After the passage of HB 2295, the Department' s Appeals Division
conducted a hearing on the Taxpayers' refund claims. It issued Deter-
mination No. 99- 351 on December 30, 1999, holding: ( 1) the Taxpayers'
failure to file applications for sales tax deferrals and B&O tax
credits prior to undertaking their investments in their apple packing
and controlled atmosphere storage business was fatal to the claim for
refund; and ( 2) the Department did not have the authority to pass on
the Taxpayers' claim that the retroactive provisions of HB 2295
infringed on their constitutional rights.
The Taxpayers timely filed Notices of Appeal with this Board.
ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
I
Beginning in 1985, Washington permitted manufacturers in loca-
tions suffering high unemployment (" distressed areas") to defer
payment of sales tax on investments in manufacturing buildings and
machinery. Laws of 1985, ch. 232. With regard to the sales tax
deferral, RCW 82. 60. 030, Laws of 1985, ch. 232, § 3, states: " Appli-
cation for deferral of taxes under this chapter must be made [ to the
Department] before initiation of the construction of the investment
project or acquisition of equipment or machinery."

The Department argues that the requirement for submitting an

The word " must" has legal consequences, and has the same effect

The Taxpayers argue that they should be entitled to refunds on
the related equitable ground of " unjust enrichment." We disagree.
First, the State Supreme Court considered " unfairness" and " manifest
injustice" when it established the rule that the government cannot be

1 OPINION
2
3 COYLE, Chair --The issue in this case is whether a purchaser of
4 farm and agricultural land is required to show, to the satisfaction
5 of the Assessor, that the land continues to qualify for open space
6 classification before the deed is recorded.
7
8 The facts are not in dispute. The matter is before us. on stipu-
9 lated facts and uncontradicted affidavits. The Ayres purchased an
10 80 -acre farm on San Juan Island. The farm had been taxed as open
11 space farm and agricultural land. The Ayres wished to continue the
12 agricultural use, and wished the property to remain in the open space
13 classification. The day before the sale transaction closed, the Ayres
14 signed a notice of continuance in open space classification. On the
15 closing day, the Ayres' representative presented the signed notice of
16 continuance to the Assessor. Because this was the first time the
17 Assessor had heard of the impending sale, he told the representative
18 that he would need more time and additional information, such as a
19 farm management plan, in order to determine if the property continued
20 to qualify for open space classification. The Ayres wished to have
21 the transaction close on that day. Therefore, they paid -the addi-
22 tional tax and penalties, and the deed was recorded.
23
24 The Ayres filed an appeal with the San Juan County Board of
25 Equalization ( Board of Equalization), seeking to have the land
26
27

1 continued in the open space classification. The Board of Equalization
2 ruled in favor of the Ayres. The Assessor appeals.
3
4 ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
5
6 Once land has been classified as open space farm and agricultural
7 land, it remains so until it ceases to be used for farm purposes ( RCW
84. 34. 080) or until certain events take place. One of those events is
9 the sale of the property to a new owner. RCW 84. 34. 108( 1)( c) requires
10 the Assessor to remove the land from open space classification upon:
11 Sale or transfer of all or a portion of such land to
a new owner, unless the new owner has signed a notice of
12 classification continuance, except transfer to an owner who
is an heir or devisee of a deceased owner shall not, by
13 itself, result in removal of classification. The notice of
continuance shall be on a form prepared by the department
14 of revenue. If the notice of continuance is not signed by
the new owner and attached to the real estate excise tax
15 affidavit, all additional taxes calculated pursuant to sub-
section ( 4) of this section shall become due and payable
16 by the seller or transferor at time of sale. The county
auditor shall not accept an instrument of conveyance of
17 classified land for filing or recording unless the new owner
has signed the notice of continuance or the additional tax
18 has been paid, as evidenced by the real estate excise- tax
stamp affixed thereto by the treasurer. The seller, trans-
19 feror, or new owner may appeal the new assessed valuation
calculated under subsection ( 4) of this section to the
20 county board of equalization. Jurisdiction is hereby con-
ferred on the county board of equalization to hear these
21 appeals . . . .
22
23 The Department of Revenue ( Department) has adopted rules to
24 implement this statute. The relevant rule, WAC 458- 30- 275, states:
25 1) Introduction. When land classified under chapter
84. 34 RCW is sold or transferred certain procedures must
26 be followed if the new owner wishes to keep the land in

b) " Notice of continuance" means the notice signed

8 or transferred and when the new owner of the classified land

9 sions of chapter 84. 34 RCW. This notice may be either part

c) " Owner" means any person or persons having a fee

of this section for a discussion regarding this affidavit);
18 and

to continue its eligibility for classification under the
20 provisions of chapter 84. 34 RCW; and
c) Sign a separate notice of continuance prepared by
21 the department if the county has decided that it will require
new owners to submit such a form.
22 4) Assessor' s duties and authority related to sale or
transfers. When land classified under chapter 84. 34 RCW is
23 in the process of being sold or transferred, the new _owner
must sign a notice of continuance and the statement described
24 in subsection ( 3) of this section if he or she wishes the
land to remain classified. This notice of continuance and
25 signed statement shall be presented to the assessor who must
determine if the land will continue to be used in a manner
26 approved for classified status or if the land will not be
27

1 used in a manner consistent with the current use program.
The assessor shall be allowed a reasonable amount of time
2 to determine whether the classified use of the land will be
continued by the new owner.
3 a) Upon receipt of the notice of classification
continuance, the assessor may require the new owner to submit
4 additional information including, but not limited to, the
types of data listed in WAC 458- 30- 270.
5 b) Within fifteen calendar days of receiving the
notice of classification continuance, the signed statement,
6 and all requested information, the assessor shall determine
whether the land qualifies for continued classification as of

8 ity to determine if the land will qualify for continued clas-
sification. The assessor and/ or the granting authority may

d) No instrument of conveyance may be filed with the
11 county auditor or recorded unless:

13 ii) If the land is no longer eligible to be classi-

iv) In the case of a sale, a completed real estate

20 chapter 84. 34 RCW.

22 assessor shall:
i) Follow the standard procedures set forth in WAC

24 ii) Notify the county treasurer and the seller or

25 penalty are due as a result of the sale or transfer because
RCW 84. 34. 108( 5) specifically exempts the transaction from

the imposition of additional tax, applicable interest, and
penalty; and
iii) In the case of land acquired for conservation
purposes by any of the entities listed in RCW 84. 34. 108( 5)
f), inform the new owner or transferee that if the land
ceases to be used for the purposes enumerated in RCW 84. 34-
210 or 64. 04. 130, the additional tax, applicable interest,
and penalty will be due.
5) Timber land. When a parcel( s) of classified
timber land is sold or transferred, the new owner must submit
a timber management plan to the assessor in order to continue
the classification, in addition to the general requirements
listed in subsection ( 3) of this section. The assessor shall
send a copy of the timber management plan to the county
legislative authority of the county in which the classified
land is located. WAC 458- 30- 232 contains a list of the types
of additional information an assessor may require the new
owner to submit so that the assessor can determine if the
land will continue to be used to grow and harvest forest
crops for commercial purposes.
6) Farm and agricultural land. When a parcel( s) of
classified. farm and agricultural land is sold or transferred,
the new owner must comply with the general requirements set
forth in subsection ( 3) of this section. The size of the
parcel( s) of farm and agricultural land sold or transferred
will determine whether any additional requirements must also
be satisfied. A parcel( s) of land that is less than twenty
acres must produce a specified amount of income to remain
classified as farm and agricultural land. After all required
information is submitted, the assessor shall determine
whether the land qualifies for continued classification..
a) Twenty acres or more. If the parcel( s) sold or
transferred is twenty acres or more, the new owner must
satisfy the general requirements listed in subsection ( 3) of
this section.
b) Less than twenty acres. In a sale or transfer
involving less than twenty acres, the new owner will be
required to comply with the general requirements of sub-
section ( 3) of this section and may be asked to provide gross
income data relating to the productivity of the farm or
agricultural operation for three of the past five years.
This information regarding the earning or productive capacity
of the classified land will be used to determine if the land
meets the income criteria listed in chapter 84. 34 RCW and
this WAC chapter.
i) Minimum income limits are set forth in RCW 84-
34. 020( 2) ( b) ( i) and ( ii) for parcels that are at least five
but less than twenty acres in size and in RCW 84. 34. 020( 2)
c)( i) and ( ii) for parcels that are less than five acres in
size. Any sale or transfer of classified land, except to a
surviving spouse, subject to these income limits. See WAC

458- 30- 210( 3) and 458- 30- 317 for further information and
details.
ii) If, after January 1, 1993, classified land is sold
by an owner who applied for and was granted classification
prior to January 1, 1993, to a new owner, the minimum income
requirements specified in RCW 84. 34. 020( 2)( b)( ii) and ( c)( ii)
will be deferred for a period of three years. The new owner
must meet these minimum income limits at least once during
the three calendar years immediately following the sale or
transfer of the classified farm and agricultural land. For
example, if classification was granted in 1978 to a fifteen
acre parcel that produced a gross income of one hundred
thirty dollars per acre per year and the land is sold on
April 15, 1993, the minimum income requirements will be
deferred until 1996. By the end of 1996, the new owner must
provide proof that the parcel produced two hundred dollars
per acre at least one year during the three-year period
between 1993 and 1996. If the land has produced a. gross
income of two hundred dollars per acre the land will remain
classified as farm and agricultural land. If the land has
not produced this amount at least once during this three-year
period, the land shall be removed from classification and the
owner will be required to pay an additional tax, interest,
and penalty.
iii) If, after January 1, 1993, classified land is
sold by an owner who applied for and was granted classifi-
cation after January 1, 1993, the assessor will review the
information regarding the productivity of the land for three
out of the past five years to determine whether the minimum
income limits set forth in RCW 84. 34. 020( 2)( b)( ii) or ( c)( ii)
have been met. For example, if a ten acre parcel was granted
classification on May 1, 1993, and it is sold on February 23,
1994, the assessor will ask the seller and/ or buyer of the
classified land to provide information about the earning or
production capacity of the land for at least the five calen-
dar years preceding the sale ( i.e., 1989 through 1993). To
retain the current use classification, the land must have
produced a minimum of two hundred dollars per acre per year
at least three out of the five calendar years preceding the
date of sale.
c) Segregation of land. In a sale or transfer
involving a land segregation, the owner of the newly created
parcel( s), and the owner of the parcel( s) of land from which
the segregated land was taken must comply with the require-
ments of ( a) or ( b) of this subsection before the assessor
determines if the land qualifies for continued classifica-
tion.
7) New owner' s warranty. The new owner, upon signing
the notice of continuance, warrants that future use of the
land will conform to the provisions of chapter 84. 34 RCW and
this WAC chapter.

8) Real estate excise tax. Under the provisions of
chapter 82. 45 RCW whenever real property is sold or trans-
ferred an excise tax is imposed; the amount of this tax is
related to the selling price of the real property. Real
estate excise tax is due at the time of sale. This tax is
paid to and collected by the treasurer of the county where
the real property is located.
a) The seller or the buyer, or the agent of either,
of the real property must pay the excise tax and must submit
a signed real estate excise tax affidavit to the treasurer of
the county where the real property is located.
b) When the ownership of classified land is sold or
transferred to a new owner who intends to continue classifi-
cation of the land under the provisions of chapter 84. 34 RCW,
the new owner must make a notation of this intent on the
affidavit.
c) No instrument of sale or conveyance evidencing a
sale subject to the real estate excise tax may be accepted
by the county auditor for filing or recording until a stamp
is affixed to the affidavit by the treasurer that shows the
tax has been paid. The county treasurer shall not stamp the
instrument of sale or conveyance unless the assessor has
determined that the classified use of the land will be
continued or that the additional tax, interest, and/ or
penalty required under RCW 84. 34. 080 and 84. 34. 108, except
as exempted under RCW 84. 34. 070 or 84. 34. 108( 5), have been
collected.
Emphasis supplied.)
The statute, RCW 84. 34. 108( 1)( c) requires that the new owner file
a " notice of continuance" before the deed can be recorded with the
County Auditor. The main purpose of the statutory requirement for
filing a notice of continuance is to prevent the sort of unwelcome
surprise that results from being unaware that one' s newly purchased
land has previously been taxed under the Open Space Tax Act. If an
unwitting purchaser changes the use of the land, either intentionally,
such as by developing it for residential use, or unintentionally, such
as by ceasing to actively farm it, there will be a big property tax

bill forthcoming, which the purchaser did not consider when negoti-
ating a purchase price with the seller.
The statute says nothing about the Assessor having to review
the notice of continuance, approve the continued use of the property
for farm and agricultural purposes prior to recording the deed, or
otherwise participate in the sale of the property in any manner. The
Assessor argues that WAC 458- 30- 275( 4), however, interposes him in the
transaction. The rule states:
d) No instrument of conveyance may be filed with the
county auditor or recorded unless:
i) The assessor has determined that the land will be
used for current use purposes and can continue to be classi-
fied within the current use program;
or ( iv) In the case of a sale, a completed real estate
excise tax affidavit has been submitted to the treasurer of
the county in which the classified land is located. To be
complete the real estate excise tax affidavit must indicate
whether the land is classified under the provisions of
chapter 84. 34 RCW.
The question before us is whether the rule requires the Assessor
to sign off on the continued taxation of the property under the Open
Space Tax Act before the County Auditor can record the deed.
Before turning to this question, we first consider our authority
to consider the Ayres' argument that the rule is inconsistent with
legislative intent or in excess of the Department' s authority to
promulgate. The Assessor argues that this Board has no authority
to declare a rule adopted by the Department invalid for any reason.
See Seattle v. Department of Ecology, 37 Wn. App. 819, 683 P. 2d 244

1984); Snohomish County v. State, 69 Wn. App. 655, 850 P. 2d 546
1993) .
3
4 We need not decide this issue because this case is before us on
5 appeal from a decision of the Board of Equalization. The question is
6 whether the Board of Equalization has the authority to ignore or
7 declare invalid a rule promulgated by the Department. There is no
8 statute which expressly, or by necessary implication, gives the Board
9 of Equalization the authority to overturn or ignore the Department' s
10 rules. In fact, RCW 84. 08. 120 provides: " It shall be the duty of
11 every public officer to comply with any lawful order, rule or regu-
12 lation of the department of revenue made under the provisions of this
13 title."
14
15 We therefore conclude the Board of Equalization has no authority
16 to ignore the Department' s rules. It follows that in this particular
17 appeal, we have no authority to declare the Department' s rule, WAC
18 458- 30- 275, invalid.'
19
20 The remaining question concerns the construction to be given to
21 the language of the rule. The standard rules of statutory construc-
22 tion are employed to interpret administrative rules. State -v. Burke,
23 92 Wn. 2d 474, 598 P. 2d 395 ( 1979). Where the language is plain,
24
25
26 1 Given this result, we have no need to reach the issue of whether the
Department is a necessary party to this appeal.
27

unambiguous, and clear on its face, there is no room for construc-
tion, i. e., it must be construed according to its terms. Snow' s
Mobile Homes, Inc. v. Morgan, 80 Wn. 2d 283, 494 P. 2d 216 ( 1972); Auto
Drivers & Demonstrators Union Local No. 882 v. Department of Retire-
ment Systems, 92 Wn. 2d 415, 598 P. 2d 379 ( 1979). Here, the language
of WAC 458- 30- 275( 4)( d) is clear onits face with regard to cllaassssii--
ffiieedd land which is to remain taxed according to its current use: " No
instrument of conveyance may be filed with the county auditor or
recorded unless . . . [ t] he assessor has determined that the land will
be used for current use purposes and can continue to be classified
within the current use program . . " There are no exceptions. We,
thus, have no occasion to consider whether the purpose of the Depart-
ment in erecting an additional hurdle to the conveyancing of current
use property bears any relationship to the purpose of the Legislature
in enacting RCW 84. 34. 108( 1)( c).
The Ayres argue that the language of the rule is ambiguous. They
point out that WAC 458- 30- 275( 4)( d), above, which specifies that the
County Auditor cannot accept a deed for recording unless certain steps
have been taken, is couched in the alternative, i. e., the use of the
word " or" implies that in the case of a sale of current use property,
the only condition which must be satisfied is the signing of a notice
of continuance. Viewed in isolation and giving the Ayres the benefit
of the doubt, they might be correct that the use of the word " Cr"
creates an ambiguity. However, administrative rules, like statutes,

must be construed as a whole, not piecemeal. Donovick v. Seattle -
First National Bank, 111 Wn. 2d 413, 757 P. 2d 1378 ( 1988). Another
section dealing with the real estate excise tax, WAC 458- 30- 275( 8)( c)
states:
No instrument of sale or conveyance evidencing a sale
subject to the real estate excise tax may be accepted by the
county auditor for filing or recording until a stamp is
affixed to the affidavit by the treasurer that shows the tax
has been paid. The county treasurer shall not stamp the
instrument of sale or conveyance unless the assessor has
determined that the classified use of the land will be
continued or that the additional tax, interest, and/ or
penalty required under RCW 84. 34. 080' and 84. 34. 108, except
as exempted under RCW 84. 34. 070 or 84. 34. 108( 5), have been
collected.
The language in this subsection clearly and unequivocally
requires the Assessor to first make a determination that the land
will continue to be classified under the Open Space Tax Act before any
deed is recorded. To the extent that there may be ambiguity in other
sections of the rule, subsection ( 8)( c), above, dispels any doubt
about the Department' s directive to the County Auditor concerning the
recording of a deed conveying current use property.
We therefore conclude the Board of Equalization erred when it
ordered the Assessor to classify the land as farm and agricultural
land. The plain language of the rule supports the Assessor' s actions.
He simply followed the rule as it was written. -

FINDINGS OF FACT
2
3 1. In April 1999, Mary -Susan and Frederick R. Ayre purchased
4 two parcels of land totaling approximately 80 acres on San Juan
5 Island: tax parcels 340214001 and 340123002 ( the " Property"). The
6 Property was classified as open space under the farm and agricultural
7 current use tax provisions. The Ayres wished to continue the present
8 use of the Property and to maintain the open space tax classification.
9
10 2. The closing date for the sale was April 30, 1999. On
11 April 29, 1999, the Ayres signed the closing papers including the Real
12 Estate Excise Tax Affidavit where they checked and signed the notice
13 of continuance indicating their intent to continue the present classi-
14 fication. The Ayres did not contact the Assessor' s office prior to
15 the closing date to obtain a determination that the land qualified for
16 continuation in the open space current use tax program.
17
18 3. On April 30, 1999, at approximately 10 a. m., the Assessor' s
19 Office was presented with an Excise Tax Affidavit with a signed notice
20 of continuance indicating that the land was classified as open space
21 and that the Ayres wished to continue in the open space tax program.
22 This was the first notice of the sale received by the Assessor' s
23 Office.
24
25 4. The Assessor told the person representing the escrow company
26 that he would need additional information to determine if the property
27

qualified for continuation in the program before the conveyance could
be recorded. Without that information, the Assessor said, he would
have to remove the land from the open space tax classification and
require payment of back taxes and penalties before a deed could be
recorded. He was given the name and number of Tinya Bakotich of
Security Escrow in Bellevue.
5. The Assessor then spoke with Ms. Bakotich and told her
that, in order to record the deed, he would either need a . farm plan
explaining how the land was going to be used to produce agricultural
products for commercial purposes, or he would need payment of " roll
back taxes". He was given the number of Mrs. Ayre.
6. The Assessor spoke with Mrs. Ayre who confirmed that she and
her husband wished to keep the Property in the farm and agriculture
open space classification and planned to continue the present use of
the Property, including the growing of hay, some grazing of cattle,
and the maintenance of a trout pond. The Assessor told Mrs. Ayre
that, in order to continue the classification, he would need to make a
determination based on a written farm plan before the deed could be
recorded. He said that without a written farm plan and determination
of continued eligibility, the only other alternative for the deed to
be recorded was to remove the land from the farm and agricultural open
space classification and pay the back taxes.

7. The Assessor told Mrs. Ayre that she could fax a plan to him
in order for him to make a determination as to whether the land quali-
fied. The Ayres, however, concluded that they could not provide all
the information required in a farm plan and still close the sale that
day.
8. Around mid- day, the Assessor received a call from Ms.
Bakotich that the Ayres were going to remove the property from the
open space program. The Assessor told Ms. Bakotich that he would need
to have that request in writing signed by one of the Ayres.
9. Shortly afterwards, the Assessor received a signed authori-
zation from Mrs. Ayre to remove the land from open space tax classi-
fication. The Assessor removed the property from the farm and agri-
cultural open space classification and calculated the back taxes for
both parcels. The taxes, totaling $97, 669. 59, were paid by the escrow
company on the Ayres' behalf and the conveyance was recorded that
afternoon.
10. The Ayres would not have asked that the property be removed
from current use classification but for the Assessor' s refusal to
approve the continued classification at the time he was presented with
the notice of continuance.
11. After the sale closed, the Ayres appealed to the Board of
Equalization the Assessor' s decision to require a determination on the

continuation of open space tax classification before the conveyance
was recorded, or whether a signed notice of continuance was sufficient
for him to approve the conveyance for recording.
12. The Board of Equalization ruled in favor of the Ayres. The
Assessor filed his Notice of Appeal within thirty days of the Board of
Equalization' s decision.
Any Conclusion of Law which should be deemed a Finding of Fact is
hereby adopted as such.
From these findings, this Board comes to these
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. The Board has jurisdiction over the parties and subject
matter of this appeal.
2. The issue in this appeal is ,whether a purchaser of land
classified as farm and agricultural for purposes of property taxation
according to the Open Space Tax Act, chapter 84. 34 RCW, is required to
obtain a determination from the Assessor that the land will be
eligible for continued classification as farm and agricultural land
prior to recording the deed with the County Auditor.

1 3. The statute, RCW 84. 34. 108, which deals with the sale of
2 land taxed according to its current use, requires only that the new
3 owner sign and file a notice of intent to continue the use of the
4 property in the appropriate current use classification before the
5 County Auditor can accept the deed for recording. The main purpose
6 underlying the enactment of this statutory provision is to provide
7 assurances that the buyer is aware ( 1) that the property is enrolled
8 in the current use program and ( 2) a change in use will trigger back
9 taxes and penalties.
10
11 4. The Department' s regulation, WAC 458- 30- 275, governs the
12 actions of the Assessor and the County Auditor in administering the
13 Open Space Tax Act with respect to the sale of property taxed accord-
14 ing to that act.
15
16 5. The language of the regulation is clear and unambiguous on
17 its face. It requires the Assessor to determine that the land will
18 be used for current use purposes and can continue to be classified
19 within the current use program prior to the time that any instrument
20 conveying such land can be accepted by the County Auditor for filing
21 or recording.
22
23 6. The Assessor acted in accordance with WAC 458- 30- 275 when
24 he required the purchasers to demonstrate to his satisfaction that
25 the land will be used for current use purposes and could continue to
26 be classified within the current use program before he noted such a
27

finding on the documents to be presented to the County Auditor. It
was not unreasonable for the Assessor to ask for additional informa-
tion concerning the use of the property.
7. The issue in this case is whether the Board of Equalization,
and not the Board of Tax Appeals, has the authority to ignore or
invalidate WAC 458- 30- 275.
8. The Board of Equalization has no authority to ignore or
invalidate WAC 458- 30- 275.
9. The Board of Equalization erred when it reversed the Asses-
sor' s determination.

10 This matter came before the Board of Tax Appeals ( Board) for a
11 formal hearing on June 29, 2000. Larry A. Jones, Attorney at Law,
12 appeared for Appellant, Rebecca Lynn Coomer. Margaret Pahl, Senior
13 Deputy Prosecuting Attorney, appeared for Respondent, Scott Noble,
14 King County Assessor ( Assessor).
15
16 This Board heard the testimony, reviewed the evidence, and
17 considered the arguments made on behalf of both parties. This Board
18 now makes its decision as follows:
19 EXEMPTION STATUS FOR THE 1998 ASSESSMENT YEAR
20 BOARD OF BOARD OF
EQUALIZATION TAX APPEALS

22
282607- 9026 NOT EXEMPT EXEMPT
23
24
OPINION
25
26
COYLE, Chair—The issue in this appeal is whether a severely and
27
permanently disabled child who owns a home in her own name can qualify

1 for a retired persons' property tax exemption ( RCW 84. 36. 379, et
2 seq.). The Assessor denied the exemption on the grounds that a child
3 who is too young to work cannot be " retired". We conclude that such
4 children fit within both the letter and spirit of the exemption law,
5 and overturn the Assessor' s decision.
6
7 Rebecca Lynn Coomer, age 9 ' 1, is severely disabled due to an
8 accident at birth. It is unlikely she will ever be able to work,
9 except possibly in a highly structured environment such as a sheltered
10 workshop. With a portion of the proceeds of a medical malpractice
11 settlement, Rebecca' s parents built a home specially designed for her
12 needs, and with specific court approval transferred ownership of the
13 home to Rebecca. 1 Rebecca and her family reside in the home. Her
14 mother, Sally Coomer, is Rebecca' s guardian and full-time caregiver.
15
16 The remaining proceeds of the settlement are invested, with the
17 expectation that investment income will provide some assistance in
18 meeting Rebecca' s special needs over her lifetime. The annual
19 investment income, also in Rebecca' s own name, is currently less than
20 30, 000.
21
RebeL a' b Luuit- appointed guardian ad litem explained the reasoning
22 behind this arrangement as follows: " Rebecca needs care now. She is
completely dependent on others for her safety, security, and
23
existence. If a house is built for her and designed for her
24 particular needs, and if that house can be built at cost and the title
be in the name of the guardianship so that Rebecca would benefit from
25 any increase in value, and if the house is free and clear of any
mortgage, then Rebecca will be as secure and as " safe" as she could
26 ever hope to be." Report of Guardian Ad Litem, Ervin A. DeSmet,
Regarding Proposed Allocation of Funds, In the Matter of the
27
Guardianship of Rebecca Coomer, King County Superior Court No. 95- 4-
01255- 5 ( Appellant' s post -hearing exhibit).
r,T,.,,, r .., T T .,, n i. , , nn_ n' 7

1
2 Washington provides a property tax exemption for residences owned
3 by retired persons, i.e., those who are " retired from regular gainful
4 employment by reason of disability." RCW 84. 36. 381. The Assessor
5 determined that Rebecca could not qualify for this exemption because
6 she had never worked, and "... it is clear her age would prevent her from
7 working at this time, regardless of her state of disability." ( Letter
8 from Ethel Jackson, Exemptions Coordinator, [ Ex. R- 5]). The King
9 County Board of Equalization upheld the Assessor' s determination.
10
11 ANALYSIS
12
13 The facts are not seriously in dispute. Rebecca is disabled to
14 the point where she will never be able to work, except possibly in a
15 highly structured environment such as a sheltered workshop. The
16 evidence is also undisputed that Rebecca' s annual income as of 1998
17 was less than $ 30, 000. The only issue is legal in nature: does
18 Rebecca come within the ambit of the statute granting the tax
19 exemption, i. e., is she " retired from regular gainful employment..:"?
20
21 We begin with the rules of statutory construction. The primary
22 purpose of statutory construction is to discern and give effect to the
23 intent of the legislature. Burlington Northern v. Johnston, 89 Wn. 2d
24 321 ( 1977). Where statutory language is not ambiguous, there is no
25 reason to resort to additional rules of construction: the statutory
26 language should be given its ordinary meaning. Automobile Drivers &
27 Demonstrators Union Local No. 882 v. Dept. of Retirement Systems, 92

1 Wn. 2d 415 ( 1979). In the case of ambiguity, we may examine
2 legislative history and other extrinsic aids to construction in order
3 to determine legislative intent. State ex. rel Bugge v. Martin, 38
4 Wn. 2d 834 ( 1951). In the special case of tax exemption statutes one
5 additional rule applies: tax exemption statutes should be construed
6 strictly, though fairly, in favor of the application of the tax.
7 Corporation of Catholic Archbishop of Seattle v. Johnston, 89 Wn. 2d
8 505 ( 1978). This means that if there is any ambiguity or reasonable
9 doubt about the meaning of the language used in the exemption statute,
10 it should be resolved against the claim of exemption.
11
12 The Assessor argues that the terms of the statute should be
13 construed according to their ordinary meaning. The dictionary
14 definition of " retire" is "... to withdraw from...[one' s] occupation."
15 Webster' s Third New International Dictionary Unabridged ( 1971). The
16 definition of " regular gainful employment" is " consistent or habitual
17 labor or service which results in an increase in wealth or earnings."
18 WAC 458- 16- 010( 8). The Assessor argues that Rebecca is not " retired
19 from regular gainful employment" because ( 1) she has never withdrawn
20 from a position or occupation, and ( 2) she has never engaged in an
21 activity that has resulted in an increase in wealth or earnings.
22
23 We conclude the Assessor' s construction of the statutory
24 language, although supportable, is nevertheless erroneous because ( 1)
25 it produces anomalous results, and ( 2) it fails to take into account
26 the purpose of the exemption.
27
nn nn -7

1 Under the Assessor' s construction, a person would be required to
2 work at some gainful occupation at some time in order to be eligible
3 for the exemption. 2 Yet the Assessor does not dispute that a full-time
homemaker who has never worked at all outside the home ' is eligible for
5 the exemption. This anomalous result undermines the Assessor' s
6 position.
7
8 The statutory exemption has its roots in. Art. VII, sec. 10 of the
9 Washington Constitution, which states in pertinent part:
10 The legislature shall have the power, by appropriate
legislation, to grant to retired property owners relief from
11 the property tax on the real property occupied as a
residence by those owners. The legislature may place such

1 ISSUE
2
3 BRYDON, Chair --Does a parcel whose current use classification is
4 derived through its " integral" link to a noncontiguous but commonly
5 owned farm parcel retain its farm and agricultural land classification
6 on sale of the farm parcel to a separate owner, there being no change
7 to the " integral" link between the properties after the sale?
8
9 We conclude that where the integral relationship of the parcels
10 is unchanged upon sale, there is no requirement to alter the current
11 use classification, solely due to the change in ownership.
12
13 FACTS
14
15 The facts are not in dispute and are summarized as follows. The
16 subject property is a five -acre parcel located on Sorenson Road in
17 Kittitas County, Assessor' s Parcel No. 17- 20- 2000- 0012. The parcel is
18 unimproved other than for boundary fencing and work done in 1986 to

21

23 co- owner, a second, 175 -acre property known as Willow Springs Ranch
24 Ranch)' located approximately one- quarter mile to the west. 2 The two

The intervening land between the Ranch and subject is comprised

12

16 for its domestic ( residential), agricultural, and livestock water
17 needs.

3 We begin our analysis with the Assessor' s central contention that
4 on sale of the Ranch, the retained subject property is no longer part

10 follows:

12 twenty or more acres:

established by rule . . . .

6 It is axiomatic that farm and agriculture operations are
7 dependent on a viable water source. No water, no farm. The testimony

13 ment of common ownership of the noncontiguous parcels. Therefore, the
14 Board concludes that subject parcel with its sole source water supply
15 is central to the farming operations conducted on the Ranch and,
16 therefore, an integral part of farming operations conducted on land
17 classified as open space farm and agricultural lands.

24 following sale. On that basis, the Board concludes subject parcel

court: Washington State Board of Tax Appeals
title: NICK URAGA and LESLEY GOODSON v. Washington Dept. of Revenue (BTA Docket No. 00-065)
text:
BEFORE THE BOARD OF TAX APPEALS
STATE OF WASHINGTON
NICK URAGA and )
LESLEY GOODSON, )
Docket No. 00- 065
Appellants, )
RE: Property Tax Appeal
v. ) Destroyed Property
KEN MADSEN, ) FINAL DECISION
Pierce County )
Assessor/ Treasurer, )
Respondent. )
This matter came before the Board of Tax Appeals ( Board) for a
formal hearing on August 28, 2001. Nick Uraga appeared for Appel-
lants, Nick Uraga and Lesley Goodson ( Owners). David Prather, Deputy
Prosecuting Attorney, appeared for Respondent, Ken Madsen, Pierce
County Assessor/ Treasurer ( Assessor).
This Board heard the testimony, reviewed the evidence, and
considered the arguments made on behalf of both parties. This Board
now makes its decision as follows:
VALUATION FOR THE 1999 ASSESSMENT YEAR
BOARD OF BOARD OF
EQUALIZATION TAX APPEALS
PARCEL NO. VALUATION VALUATION
5930030350 NOT EXEMPT NOT EXEMPT
OPINION
This is an appeal from a decision of the Pierce County Board of
Equalization denying the Owners' application for a destroyed property

1 exemption ( RCW 84. 70. 010, et. seq.). The Owners had built their home
2 in violation of neighborhood covenants. Shortly after the valuation
3 date, the Pierce County Superior Court prohibited the Owners from
4 occupying the home, and ordered it torn down to the foundation. The
5 home remained standing—but unoccupied and boarded up—pending appeal.
6 We conclude the destroyed property exemption does not apply to a home
7 which is under a judicial order of destruction so long as the home
8 remains physically intact while an appeal is pending. We affirm the
9 decision of the Board of Equalization.
10
11 FACTS
12
13 The essential facts are not in dispute. The Owners built their
14 home beginning in 1998 in a subdivision overlooking the Tacoma
15 Narrows. The neighborhood covenants required a roof pitch no greater
16 than 2 feet of rise for every 12 feet of run, except where the
17 subdivision' s architectural control committee determined that a
18 greater roof pitch would not impair or destroy the view of neighboring
19 properties. For reasons which are not relevant to the issue before
20 us, the Owners did not receive the approval of the architectural
21 control committee before constructing the home. The neighbors sued,
22 and on August 10, 1999, the Pierce County Superior Court verbally
23 prohibited the Owners from occupying the home, and ordered it torn
24 down to its foundation. The verbal order was reduced to writing and
25 entered as a judgment on December 3, 1999.
26
27
FINAL DECISION - Page 2 Docket No. 00- 065

1 The Assessor had assessed the home in 1999 as new construction,
2 with a valuation date of July 31, 1999. At the time the Assessor made
3 his valuation, he considered the home 90 percent complete. He did not
4 know of the lawsuit. He sent a Change of Value notice to the Owners
5 in September 1999, listing an improvement value of $ 236, 000. The
6 Owners did not timely appeal this valuation to the Board of
7 Equalization, as permitted by RCW 84. 40. 038. Instead, after the
8 Superior Court entered its written order in December, 1999, the Owners
9 filed an application with the Assessor claiming a destroyed property
10 exemption pursuant to RCW Ch. 84. 70. The Assessor denied the
11 application because the home remained standing. The Board of
12 Equalization affirmed, stating:
13 This Board determines that lack of occupancy does not alone
effect the value of the property. While on court appeal,
14 the structure was standing of 7- 31- 99, and is still
standing.
15
16 ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
17
18 Since 1974 Washington has provided relief to property owners
19 whose property has been destroyed in whole or in part during the
20 assessment year. The relief is in the form of a reduction in the
21 property' s assessed value, applied on a pro rata basis depending on
22 the date the property was damaged or destroyed. The statute, RCW
23 84. 70. 010, provides in relevant part:
24 1) If, on or before December 31 in any calendar year, any
real or personal property placed upon the assessment roll of
25 that year is destroyed in whole or in part, or is in an area
that has been declared a disaster area by the governor and
26 has been reduced in value by more than twenty percent as a
result of a natural disaster, the assessed value of such
27 property shall be reduced for that assessment year by an
amount determined by taking the assessed value of such
FINAL DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 00- 065

1 taxable property before destruction or reduction in value
and deduct therefrom the true and fair value of the
2 remaining property after destruction or reduction in value.
3
4
The Owners argue that their home has been " destroyed" within the
5
meaning of the statute because as of August 10, 1999 they could not
6
occupy it, and were under a court order to tear it down to the
7
foundation. The Owners cite the definition of " destroyed" from the
8
Random House Dictionary: "... to reduce to...a useless form or remains...to
9
render ineffective or useless...." They contend that the Superior
10
Court' s oral ruling prohibiting occupancy rendered their home useless
11
as of August 10, 1999, effectively " destroying" it.
12
13
The Assessor also cites the Random House Dictionary definition of
14
destroy". He argues that although the Superior Court' s order might
15
have rendered the property useless, it did not " destroy" the Owners'
16
property because the Owners had no property right to build the home in
17
violation of the neighborhood covenants in the first instance. The
18
Assessor thus focuses not on the physical components of the property,
19
but on the intangible property rights associated with the ownership of
20
the property. The Assessor further argues that even if the Superior
21
Court' s order " destroyed" the property, the destruction did not occur
22
until December 3, 1999, when the court reduced its oral decision to
23
its final written judgment. State v. Dailey, 93 Wn. 2d 454 ( 1980).
24
25
We begin our analysis by noting that the issue is one of
26
statutory construction of a statute granting an exemption from
27
taxation. Our duty is to ascertain and give effect to the purpose and
FINAL DECISION - Page 4 Docket No. 00- 065

1 intent of the legislature, as expressed in the act. Burlington
2 Northern, Inc. v. Johnston, 89 Wn. 2d 321 ( 1977). Legislative intent
3 is to be first deduced from the statutory language. In re Lyon' s
4 Estate, 83 Wn. 2d 105 ( 1973). The words of a statute, unless otherwise
5 defined, must be given their ordinary meaning. Pope & Talbot, Inc. v.
6 State Dept. of Revenue, 90 Wn. 2d 191 ( 1978). In the case of
7 ambiguity, statutes granting an exemption from taxation should be
8 strictly, but fairly, construed against the claim of exemption. Group
9 Health Co- op of Puget Sound, Inc. v. Washington State Tax Com' n, 72
10 Wn. 2d 422 ( 1967).
11
12 The common everyday meaning of the term " destroy" is set out in
13 Webster' s Third New International Dictionary, Unabridged ( 1971), as
14 follows:
15 1. To ruin the structure, or organic existence of, or
condition of, as: a: to pull or tear down: RAZE,
16 DEMOLISH...c: to ruin completely or injure or mutilate
beyond possibility of use ( as be tearing, breaking,
17 burning, erosion.... Destroy implies any force that
smashes, tears down or apart, kills, annihilates
18 destroy a house> < destroy a document by burning it>
destroy a friendship by deceit> < destroy a bridge by
19 blowing it up.>
20
The term " destroy" thus means more than merely " rendering useless."
21
It implies physical demolition beyond possibility of further use.
22
This is the sense that the Assessor and the Board of Equalization
23
understood the term, and we agree. The purpose of the destroyed
24
property exemption, is to eliminate the perceived unfairness of
25
requiring a property owner to shoulder the burden of supporting
26
government services ( e. g., police and fire protection) which do not,
27
and cannot, benefit the owner' s property. So long as the property
FINAL DECISION - Page 5 Docket No. 00- 065

1 remains in existence it benefits from the full range of governmental
2 services. Therefore, a grant of exemption is inconsistent with the
3 purpose of the exemption. We thus conclude that the term " destroyed
4 property" is limited to property which is physically demolished in
5 whole or in part.
6
7 Further, we are far from convinced that the Owner' s property has
8 been " destroyed" in any sense of the term by the Superior Court' s
9 order. As of the close of the assessment year, December 31, 1999, the
10 Superior Court' s order was on appeal, and its effect had been stayed.
11 The Owners understandably hoped that the order would be reversed on
12 appeal, or at least modified in such a manner that most of the
13 structure would remain in existence. Thus, even if the term
14 destroyed" is understood to mean " rendered useless," the Owners' home
15 had not been finally, irrevocably, and certainly placed in that
16 condition as of the close of assessment year 1999. So long as an
17 appeal remains pending, the property cannot qualify for the destroyed
18 property exemption.
19
20 For the foregoing reasons, we uphold the determination of the
21 Board of Equalization.
22
23
24
25 FINDINGS OF FACT
26 1. This is an appeal from a decision of the Pierce County Board of
27 Equalization. The Owners filed their Notice of Appeal with this Board
FINAL DECISION - Page 6 Docket No. 00- 065

1 within 30 days of the filing of the Board of Equalization' s written
2 decision. The Assessor requested that the proceeding be held as a
3 formal appeal, pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act, RCW Ch.
4 34. 05.
5
6 2. The property which is the subject of this appeal is a single
7 family home located at 2512 N. Vista View Dr., Tacoma, Washington.
8 The Owners built their home beginning in 1998. The neighborhood
9 covenants required a roof pitch no greater than 2 feet of rise for
10 every 12 feet of run, except where the subdivision' s architectural
11 control committee determined that a greater roof pitch would not
12 impair or destroy the view of neighboring properties.
13
14 3. The Owners did not receive the approval of the architectural
15 control committee before constructing the home. The Owners' neighbors
16 filed an action in court seeking to enjoin the construction of the
17 home. On August 10, 1999, the Pierce County Superior Court verbally
18 prohibited the Owners from occupying the home, and ordered it torn
19 down to its foundation. The verbal order was reduced to writing and
20 entered as a judgment on December 3, 1999. The Owners filed a
21 supersedeas bond and appealed the Superior Court' s decision to the
22 Court of Appeals. As of the date of the hearing, the Court of Appeals
23 had rendered a decision upholding the Superior Court' s order, and the
24 case was on appeal to the Washington Supreme Court. The home remains
25 standing, but it is boarded up and unoccupied.
26
27
FINAL DECISION - Page 7 Docket No. 00- 065

1 4. The Assessor had assessed the home in 1999 as new construction,
2 with a valuation date of July 31, 1999. At the time the Assessor made
3 his valuation, he considered the home 90 percent complete. He did not
4 know of the lawsuit. He sent a Change of Value notice to the Owners
5 in September 1999, listing an improvement value of $ 236, 000. After
6 the Superior Court entered its written order in December, 1999, the
7 Owners filed an application with the Assessor claiming a destroyed
8 property exemption pursuant to RCW Ch. 84. 70. The Assessor denied the
9 application because the home remained standing. The Board of
10 Equalization affirmed the Assessor' s decision.
11
12 Any Conclusion of Law which should be deemed a Finding of Fact is
13 hereby adopted as such.
14
15 From these findings, this Board comes to these
16
17 CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
18
19 1. The Board has jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of
20 this appeal.
21
22 2. The legal issue is one of statutory construction of a statute
23 granting an exemption from taxation. The Board is required to adhere
24 to the rules of statutory construction. The main purpose of statutory
25 construction is to ascertain and give effect to the purpose and intent
26 of the legislature. Legislative intent is to be first deduced from
27 the statutory language.
FINAL DECISION - Page 8 Docket No. 00- 065

1
2 3. The words of a statute, unless otherwise defined, must be given
3 their ordinary meaning. In the case of ambiguity, statutes granting
4 an exemption from taxation should be strictly, but fairly, construed
5 against the claim of exemption.
6
7 4. The purpose of the destroyed property exemption is to eliminate
8 the perceived unfairness of requiring a property owner to shoulder the
9 burden of supporting government services ( e. g., police and fire
10 protection) which do not, and cannot, benefit the owner' s property.
11 So long as the property remains in existence it benefits from the full
12 range of governmental services. Therefore, a grant of exemption is
13 inconsistent with the purpose of the exemption.
14
15 5. The term " destroy" as used in the destroyed property exemption,
16 RCW 84. 70. 010, means physical demolition beyond possibility of further
17 use. The term " destroyed property" as used in RCW Ch. 84. 70 is
18 limited to property which is physically demolished in whole or in
19 part.
20
21 6. The Owners' home does not qualify for the destroyed property
22 exemption, RCW Ch. 84. 70, because it was physically in existence as of
23 the last day of the 1999 assessment year and because the judicial
24 order requiring it to be torn down to its foundation was stayed
25 pending appeal.
26
27
FINAL DECISION - Page 9 Docket No. 00- 065

7. The decision of the Pierce County Board of Equalization should be
affirmed.
Any Finding of Fact which should be deemed a Conclusion of Law is
hereby adopted as such.
From these conclusions, this Board enters this
DECISION
In accordance with RCW 84. 08. 130, this Board sustains the
determination of the Pierce County Board of Equalization
The Pierce County Assessor/ Treasurer is hereby directed that the
assessment and tax rolls of Pierce County are to accord with and give
full effect to the provisions of this decision.
DATED this day of 2001.

court: Washington State Board of Tax Appeals
title: STEPHEN NICHOLAS, Appellant,. v. Washington Dept. of Revenue (BTA Docket No. 00-066)
text:
BEFORE THE BOARD OF TAX APPEALS
STATE OF WASHINGTON
STEPHEN NICHOLAS,
Appellant,. Docket No. 00- 066
v. RE: Excise Tax Appeal
FINAL DECISION
STATE OF WASHINGTON
DEPARTMENT OF REVENUE,
Respondent.
This matter came before the Board of Tax Appeals ( Board) for a
formal hearing on December 17, 2001. Kevin Lyon, Attorney -at -Law,
appeared for Appellant, Steven Nicholas ( Taxpayer). David M. Hankins,
Assistant Attorney General, appeared for Respondent, Department of
Revenue ( Department).
This Board heard the testimony, reviewed the evidence, and
considered the arguments made on behalf of both parties. This Board
now makes its decision as follows:
OPINION
COYLE, Member—The issue in this appeal is whether the Department
erred when, as authorized by RCW 82. 32. 145, it pierced the corporate
veil and sought to hold a corporate officer personally liable for
collected, but unpaid sales tax. We find the Department did not make
a good faith effort to determine if there was a reasonable means to

1 collect the unpaid sales tax directly from the corporation before it
2 issued its assessment, as is required by RCW 82. 32. 145( 5). We cancel
3 the assessment.
4
5 Factual Background. 1 The Taxpayer was the president of Titanic
6 Brewing Co., Inc., which operated a brewpub ( restaurant/ microbrewery)
7 business in a leased building in Olympia, Washington. The business
8 was incorporated in January 1995, and it opened for business later
9 that year. It was not successful. It became delinquent in its tax
10 reporting, and failed to timely pay over sales taxes it had collected
11 from its customers. The Titanic Brewing Co. closed its doors and
12 ceased its retail operations in June 1997.
13
14 Ms. Lori Lindstrom, the Department' s Revenue Agent handling the
15 account, testified on behalf of the Department. Ms. Lindstrom' s
16 personal knowledge of the facts prior to April 22, 1998, the date the
17 Department determined that there was no reasonable means of collecting
18 the unpaid sales tax directly from the corporation, is somewhat
19 limited. Her supervisor, the Olympia District Compliance Manager
20 DCM), was handling the Titanic Brewing Co.' s account at the time the
21 business closed in June 1997. Prior to April 1998 the DCM had
22 obtained the corporation' s calendar year 1996 profit and loss
23 statement, and the corporation' s balance sheet as of December 31,
24 1996. Prior to April 1998, Ms. Lindstrom had no personal contact with
25
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 2 Docket No. 00- 066

the Taxpayer. She took no steps to confirm the existence of the
corporate assets, or determine their condition and value, and she was
unable to discover any written record that anyone else in the
Department had done so. She made no analysis of the cost of
liquidating the assets, or any analysis of the costs that might be
incurred to recover and liquidate the assets, and could find no record
that anyone else in the Department had done so. She had performed a
browse" of the UCC filing system to determine if there were any.
parties claiming a security interest in personal property owned by
Titanic Brewing Co., Inc. She did the browse at the request of the
DCM shortly after the business closed in June, 1997. She confirmed
that there was a filed security interest, but she did not order a copy
of the filed security interest or make any further determination as to
the identity of the secured parties or their relationship to the
corporation, or the amount of the debt secured by the filing, either
originally or as of the date she did the browse. She had, at the
request of the DCM, visited the Titanic Brewing Co.' s business
premises sometime in early June 1997, and had determined that it was
closed.
The Department has an Automated Collection System ( ACS) used by
Revenue Agents to assist them in their work. One of its features is a
field where the agents record their field notes, e. g. contemporaneous
records of conversations with taxpayers, attorneys, or other agencies.
1 The facts are fully set out in the Findings of Fact section,
post.
FINAL DECISION - Page 3 Docket No. 00- 066

1 The DCM prepared the field notes. They reflect the DCM' s
2 conversations with various people concerning efforts to collect the
3 Titanic Brewing Co.' s unpaid taxes. There are no notes which reveal
4 any significant effort to investigate the status of the corporation' s
5 assets.
6
7 Ms. Lindstrom and the DCM jointly made the decision to issue a
8 Trust Funds Accountability Assessment ( TFAA) against the Taxpayer,
9 because they concluded he was a person able to control payment to the
10 Department of sales tax collected from the business' s customers.
11 The Department made its determination that there was no reasonable
12 means of collecting the tax directly from the Titanic Brewing Co. on
13 or before April 22, 1998. The DCM subsequently retired from State
14 service and did not testify at the hearing.
15
16 The Department actually issued its TFAA assessment against the
17 Taxpayer on February 16, 1999. At the time the Department issued the
18 assessment, the corporation had not been dissolved, voluntarily or
19 involuntarily, and the Taxpayer was still acting as a representative
20 of the corporation.
21
22 The Taxpayer timely appealed the assessment to the Department' s
23 Appeals Division. At the hearing before the Appeals Division, the
24 Taxpayer argued that the security interest in the corporation' s assets
25 discovered by Ms. Lindstrom in her " browse" was invalid, and that the
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 4 Docket No. 00- 066

Department therefore did in fact have a reasonable means of
collection. The Appeals Division found, apparently on the basis or
the representations of the Taxpayer or his attorney, that the security
interest had been assigned to a shareholder of the corporation who had
been engaged in a protracted battle with the Taxpayer over control of
the corporation' s business and that this shareholder was
uncooperative" with respect to the Taxpayer' s interests. Based on
this information, the Appeals Division concluded there was no
reasonable means to collect the tax from the corporation. The
Determination stated ( Ex. R- 8, p. 51):
the Department is not required to contest the security
interest, sell the property, and engage in potential
litigation with the other shareholder when potential
benefits are more than offset by the costs and risk of not
invalidating the security interest.
The Appeals Division upheld the assessment. The Taxpayer timely
filed an appeal with this Board.
ANALYSIS
The statute governing corporate officer liability for collected,
but unpaid sales tax, RCW 82. 32. 145, states:
1) Upon termination, dissolution, or abandonment of a
corporate or limited liability company business, any
officer, member, manager, or other person having control or
supervision of retail sales tax funds collected and held in
trust under RCW 82. 08. 050, or who is charged with the
FINAL DECISION - Page 5 Docket No. 00- 066

responsibility for the filing of returns or the payment of
retail sales tax funds collected and held in trust under
RCW 82. 08. 050, shall be personally liable for any unpaid
taxes and interest and penalties on those taxes, if such
officer. or other person wilfully fails to pay or to cause
to be paid any taxes due from the corporation pursuant to
chapter 82. 08 RCW. For the purposes of this section, any
retail sales taxes that have been paid but not collected
shall be deductible from the retail sales taxes collected
but not paid.
For purposes of this subsection " wilfully fails to pay
or to cause to be paid" means that the failure was the
result of an intentional, conscious, and voluntary course
of action.
2) The officer, member or manager, or other person
shall be liable only for taxes collected which became due
during the period he or she had the control, supervision,
responsibility, or duty to act for the corporation
described in subsection ( 1) of this section, plus interest
and penalties on those taxes.
3) Persons liable under subsection ( 1) of this
section are exempt from liability in situations where
nonpayment of the retail sales tax funds held in trust is
due to reasons beyond their control as determined by the
department by rule.
4) Any person having been issued a notice of
assessment under this section is entitled to the appeal
procedures under RCW 82. 32. 160, 82. 32. 170, 82. 32. 180,
82. 32. 190, and 82. 32. 200.
5) This section applies only in situations where the
department has determined that there is no reasonable means
of collecting the retail sales tax funds held in trust
directly from the corporation.
6) This section does not relieve the corporation or
limited liability company of other tax liabilities or
otherwise impair other tax collection remedies afforded by
law
7) Collection authority and procedures prescribed in
this chapter apply to collections under this section.
1995 c 318 § 2; 1987 c 245 § 1.]
1. Corporate dissolution or abandonment. The Taxpayer first
argues that the Department may not issue a TFAA until the corporation
itself has been terminated, dissolved or abandoned. Correctly
recognizing that the statutory language appears to indicate that the
FINAL DECISION - Page 6 Docket No. 00- 066

limiting factor is the termination, dissolution, or abandonment of the
corporate business, and not the corporation itself, the Taxpayer
nevertheless argues that the Department' s implementing regulation, WAC
458- 20- 217, limits the issuance of a TFAA to situations where the
corporation itself has been terminated, dissolved, or abandoned.
The Taxpayer is correct that the regulation as it existed in
February 19992 defined " termination", " abandonment", and " dissolution"
primarily in terms of the continued legal or factual existence of the
corporate entity itself. The Taxpayer' s conclusion is plausible; but
it does not withstand a close reading by a jaundiced eye. WAC 458- 20-
217( 6)( d) stated:
Requirements for assessment. Before the department
may assess trust fund accountability for retail sales tax
held in trust, the statute requires that the underlying
retail sales tax liability be that of a corporation.
Second, there must also be a termination, dissolution, or
abandonment of the corporation....
The Taxpayer' s conclusion is certainly plausible; but it does not
withstand a close reading of the rule by a jaundiced eye. The terms
termination", " abandonment", and " dissolution" were defined in WAC
458- 20- 217( 6)( c) as follows:
iii) Termination: The term " termination" means
revocation of the corporation' s certificate of
registration, the first act of liquidation or distribution
of corporate assets with the intent to cease any further
2 The regulation has since been substantially rewritten. Because the
Department does not argue otherwise, we assume the regulations as they
existed at the time the Department issued the assessment control our
analysis.
FINAL DECISION - Page 7 Docket No. 00- 066

1 business activity after liquidation or distribution, the
filing of a petition in bankruptcy court for complete
2 liquidation or any other act evidencing the intent to quit
business or close business activity.
3
iv) Abandonment: The term " abandonment" means the
4 officers, directors, and shareholders have relinquished all
dominion and control of the corporate affairs and there is
5 no one who acknowledges authority to act for or on behalf
of the corporation.
6
v) Dissolution: The term " dissolution" means
7 statutory dissolution pursuant to chapter 23A. 28 RCW.
8
The question is whether the language of the rule, fairly
9
construed, limits the Department' s authority to issue a TFAA to
10
situations where the corporation itself has been terminated,
11
abandoned, or dissolved. The rules of statutory construction apply to
12
construction of administrative rules. State v. Burke, 92 Wn. 2d 474
13
1979). An administrative rule implementing a statute should be
14
construed in a manner consistent with the legislative intent as
15
expressed in the statute. See, Hayes v. Yount, 87 Wn. 2d 280 ( 1976);
16
Downtown Traffic Planning Committee v. Royer, 26 Wn. App. 156 ( 1980).
17
The Taxpayer concedes the legislature intended that the Department' s
18
authority to issue a TFAA include situations where the business has
19
been terminated, abandoned or dissolved. The above -emphasized
20
language of the rule' s definition of " termination," "... any other act
21
evidencing the intent to quit business or close business activity", is
22
sufficiently broad to include the permanent closure of the business as
23
an act of " termination" under the rule. Here, the business was closed
24
in June 1997. By April 1998, ten months later, it had not reopened,
25
and there is no evidence of record that the Taxpayer, in his corporate
26
27 FINAL DECISION - Page 8 Docket No. 00- 066

officer capacity, ever told the Department that it would reopen. The
closure of the business in fact, the passage of time, and the lack of
any claim, let alone assurance, from the business' s owner that it
would reopen, are more than sufficient to constitute facts evidencing
an intent to " quit business or close business activity." We must
reject the Taxpayer' s argument on this point.
2) Reasonable means of collection. The Taxpayer argues the
Department must, before issuing a TFAA, determine "... that there is no
reasonable means of collecting the retail sales tax funds held in
trust directly from the corporation." RCW 82. 32. 145( 5). The Taxpayer
claims the Department made no effort to determine whether there was a
reasonable means of collecting the tax, such as investigating the
value or existence of assets of the corporation, and whether there
were competing claims against the assets.
The Department agrees that it must make a determination of
reasonableness of collection, but argues that it need not articulate
its determination until after it issues the assessment and the
individual has appealed. The Department points out that there is no
requirement that it conduct an agency in-house adjudicative process
under the Administrative Procedure Act before it issues the TFAA. To
the extent that any written articulation is required, the Department
argues that the written determination from the Department' s Appeals
Division serves this purpose.
FINAL DECISION - Page 9 Docket No. 00- 066

We find the Department must make a good faith effort to determine
if there is a reasonable means of collecting the unpaid sales tax from
the corporation before it issues a TFAA. The plain language of the
statute requires that the Department in fact make that determination
before it issues its TFAA. The statute states:
5) This section [ RCW 82. 32. 145] applies only where
the department has determined that there is no reasonable
means of collecting the retail sales tax funds held in
trust directly from the corporation.
Emphasis supplied.)
The statutory language requires the Department to in fact make a
determination. It does not say, for example: " This section only
applies where there is no reasonable means of collecting the tax."
The statutory language is couched in the past tense; not the present
tense, i. e., " only where the department determines"; or the future
tense, i.e., " only where the department will make a determination."
The Department' s own rule, WAC 458- 20- 217( 6)( d) states:
Requirements for assessment. Before the department may
assess trust fund accountability for retail sales tax held
in trust, the statute requires that...there must be no
reasonable means to collect the tax directly from the
corporation.
Emphasis supplied.)
We conclude the Legislature employed the statutory language of
subsection ( 5) with a distinct purpose: to obtain the maximum
assurance that individual liability for corporate sales tax debts
would be sought deliberately and then only as a last resort. Piercing
FINAL DECISION - Page 10 Docket No. 00- 066

1 the corporate veil to reach the assets of individual beneficial owners
2 or officers of a corporation is an extraordinary remedy, traditionally
3 available only where the individual has used the corporate form to
4 work a fraud or injustice on others. Very few government agencies
5 have this authority. 3 The extraordinary nature of the remedy is
6 compounded by the fact that the assessment and collection process
7 itself is highly summary in nature. It thus requires the Department
8 to make a special effort to adhere to the statutory standards in order
9 to avoid potential violations of the Washington and U. S. Constitution. 4

11 process. Its Field Compliance Manual, Ex. A- 22 at 75, states:

is a collection tool to be used with discretion. It is not

opportunity to be heard, and if the procedure established by existing

we conclude that the Department' s determination must be made in good
faith, i.e., with consideration of the all facts and circumstances
after a reasonably diligent investigation. It would defeat the
legislative purpose of subsection ( 5) to permit the Department to
issue a TFAA without doing any investigation --or a wholly cursory one-
as to the likelihood of collection success against corporate assets.
What constitutes a " reasonably diligent" investigation differs
according to the circumstances of each case. At a minimum, it should
include attempts to discover ( 1) whether corporate assets exist, ( 2)
their nature ( real property, personal property, intangibles) ( 3) their
whereabouts, ( 4) their estimated liquidation value, and ( 5) whether
any other parties have competing claims, and the amount thereof.
The Department need not in every case perform a full dress
cost/ benefit analysis, or fully investigate and evaluate subjective
factors such as the nature or viability of the competing claims, the
likelihood of success in litigation, or the likely costs of
litigation.5
The Taxpayer' s expert witness, Mr. Siminski, a Certified Public
Accountant, testified that the Department should develop a
standardized methodology for handling the issuance of TFAA' s,
including a written analysis listing the various factors considered by
the Department, including what he termed " non -quantifiable factors."
Although we did admit his testimony, we accord it no weight because he
does not possess any expertise concerning the collection of tax debts
from corporations beyond that already possessed by the Board of Tax
Appeals as a result of our experience and training in matters of state
and local taxation. RCW 82. 03. 020. Although it is undoubtedly true
that requiring the Department to make a formal written analysis would
